query: For Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state, the factors governing its phase stability during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure are not understood well enough to account for the range of phases that may appear. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain this behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations relative to that baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, cooling from the high-temperature disordered BCC state induces thermally driven local chemical ordering, primarily via Cr segregation that nucleates nanoscale ordered (B2-type) precipitates. This evolving microstructure mediates the apparent wide phase variability during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, high-temperature disordered BCC phase.
generation.intervention: Performing controlled thermal treatments that vary the cooling rate and include an isothermal hold at an intermediate temperature where diffusion is moderate.
generation.conditions: The mechanism is expected to be active under conditions where atomic diffusion is sufficiently activated to allow local concentration fluctuations (e.g., moderate cooling rates and intermediate annealing temperatures). It should not be observed during ultra-rapid quenching (which would freeze the high-temperature state) or under prolonged high-temperature exposure (where complete homogenization might occur).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoscale B2 precipitates enriched in Cr, emerging within the disordered BCC matrix through local chemical ordering.
generation.mechanism: As the alloy cools, thermally activated diffusion allows Cr atoms—present in high concentration—to locally cluster. These clusters lower the local free energy by adopting an ordered B2 structure, which competes with the metastable disordered BCC state. The balance between diffusion kinetics and the thermodynamic driving force for ordering results in an inhomogeneous mixture of phases observed during subsequent thermal exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples subjected to controlled cooling (with an isothermal hold) are predicted to develop a population of nanoscale B2 precipitates with detectable Cr segregation. This contrasts with rapidly quenched samples that should remain largely as a single disordered BCC phase. Consequently, differences in properties such as hardness or ductility (e.g., a ductile-to-brittle transition) may be measurable between the two conditions.
generation.baseline: Rapidly quenched specimens that retain the high-temperature disordered BCC structure with minimal local chemical ordering.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies under thermal processing conditions that allow moderate atomic mobility. In regimes of ultra-fast quenching (insufficient time for diffusion) or extreme temperatures that lead to full re-homogenization, the predicted local ordering will not be observed.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of Cr segregation and the critical temperature/time window for B2 nucleation remain uncertain. Further quantitative analysis is needed to determine the typical size, distribution, and volume fraction of the ordered precipitates.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples from the high-temperature BCC phase. One set will be rapidly quenched to lock in the disordered structure (baseline), and the other set will be cooled at a controlled rate with an isothermal hold at an intermediate temperature that allows moderate diffusion. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) along with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to compare the presence and distribution of nanoscale ordered (B2) regions and Cr segregation. Additionally, mechanical tests (e.g., microhardness, tensile ductility) will help correlate microstructural differences with property changes.
measurements: TEM imaging to identify nanoscale precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the controlled thermal treatment samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in nanoscale B2 precipitates or Cr segregation relative to the rapidly quenched baseline, and if their mechanical properties do not differ in the predicted manner, the hypothesis is falsified.

The classical “temper embrittlement” phenomenon [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ] —documented for over a century in conventional steels and other alloys—occurs upon exposure to specific temperature ranges, sharply reducing toughness and endangering engineering safety in critical applications such as aerospace, shipping, and petrochemical systems. [ [8] , [9] , [10] ] Temper embrittlement degradation is primarily attributed to the segregation of embrittling elements or the precipitation of brittle phases along grain boundaries (GBs), which act as stress concentrators and crack initiation sites, ultimately inducing brittle fracture under stress. [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [7] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ] This well‐established mechanism highlights the central role of brittle phase precipitation and element segregation at GBs in governing embrittlement in conventional alloys.

In summary, our study deciphers an unusual ductile−brittle−ductile transition in a eutectic HEA, driven by the dynamic evolution of LCOs and PBs configurations. Enhanced LCOs and the formation of jagged PBs lead to brittleness, while controlling the order degree of LCOs and the formation of a ductile transition zone along the PBs recovers the ductility. This discovery highlights the critical role of nanoscale chemical heterogeneities and PBs in determining material behavior, challenging and expanding the traditional paradigm of thermal embrittlement. Although LCOs are generally beneficial for strength‐ductility synergy in HEAs, our findings reveal their dual role: excessive ordering induces brittleness, whereas controlled LCOs restore ductility, which further indicates the necessity of meticulous control of LCOs for better performance. We believe that the uncover of thermal evolution behavior of HEA will advance the high‐temperature application of the HEA family.
